Change 18 · revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”Why walk refuses overloads on two instantiations

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”, line 28

The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97). It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion, so it does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as at Tg[\3\] and Tg[\4\] g(b: Tg[\3\]) beside g(b: Tg[\4\]), because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule “Not allowed”: do not copy them.

Why. The sentence used “exclusion” in two senses: the rule that no type extends two instantiations of one trait, and two parameter types that exclude each other. A reader could take it that walk refuses such overloads on purpose. The text now says that walk does not apply the rule, and that it refuses the two overloads because it does not read their types as excluding each other. The cold read then had the example written as two overloads, as interpreter.md writes it, in place of two bare types.

Change 19 · revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”An example for the second kind of self-typed trait

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”, line 39, the second condition of a self-typed trait

  • T has a parameter X bounded by T itself, as trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\] (P-146), or by a self-typed trait U[\X\] that T extends at X. extends, as trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\].

Why. “A self-typed trait that T extends at X” read two ways: X bounded by U[\X\] where T extends U[\X\], or T extending U at some other argument. The text now names the trait U[\X\] and gives the first reading as an example, which is the form that walk's code describes.

Change 20 · revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”Walk now loads the self-typed pair in a program's own code

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”, lines 43 to 46

When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of T, self has the type T[\X\], except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There self has the intersection type of T[\X\] and X (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads (“Dispatch and overloading”), the library's generic + and - between an array and a number are valid beside AdditiveGroup's own. Walk loads the library's pairs, but refuses such a pair where a program's own component declares both (row 804). Walk reads self in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. Walk's load check, which is not the verdict (“Dispatch and overloading”), still refuses the pair in two cases:

  • T is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
  • T's method has static parameters of its own.

Why. The batch fixed walk's load check: walk now reads self of a self-typed trait as the checker does when it tests whether two domains exclude each other. So a program's own generic + or - between an array and a number now loads beside AdditiveGroup's, as the library's pairs did already. The old text said that walk refuses such a pair in a program, which is no longer true, so a worker would have kept a test of a failure that is gone. The text now says that walk loads the pair, and names the two cases in which its load check still refuses it. It calls that check “not the verdict”, as the part's first section does, since the checker decides whether a pair is valid. After the cold read, the second case reads “T's method”, since “the method” did not say whose.

Change 21 · revival-changes.md, “Static parameters, where clauses and sizes”“Accepts” in place of “compiles”

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

revival-changes.md, “Static parameters, where clauses and sizes”, line 70, its fourth sentence

The code generator compiles accepts a declaration's own where clause and but emits no code for it, so the compiled run time does not check it.

Why. “Compiles” reads as though code is generated for the clause, which the same sentence then denies. The code generator takes such a declaration without an error and generates nothing for the clause, so the sentence now says that it accepts the clause but emits no code for it.

Change 22 · revival-changes.md, “Numbers”Tied declarations that differ at a numeral's position

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

revival-changes.md, “Numbers”, line 82, its last sentence

Where the tied declarations differ only where the call passes a numeral, at the positions of the call's numerals, the checker reads the numeral as ZZ32, or ZZ64 or ZZ where the value does not fit.

Why. “Differ only where the call passes a numeral” could mean that the declarations differ only at the numeral's position, or only when a numeral is passed. The first is meant, and the text now says so.

Change 23 · revival-changes.md, “Reductions and comprehensions”What the team's tests do that is not to be copied

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

revival-changes.md, “Reductions and comprehensions”, line 98, its last sentence

The team's tests do so: declare simpleJoin so: do not copy them.

Why. “Do so” could point to either of the two sentences before it: the declaration at Any or untyped, or a generic reduction that stops at its first join. The sentence now names what the tests do: they declare simpleJoin at Any or untyped.

Change 24 · revival-changes.md, “Implementation limits”The fact and the plan in two sentences

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

revival-changes.md, “Implementation limits”, line 102, its bold rule and the sentence after it

Walk has no static types until it runs the checker after the switch-over (P-12). Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses.

Why. The bold rule tied a fact of today to a plan, and stated the plan as a fact. Elsewhere the skill describes the switch-over only as the compiled path's move onto the interpreter's library, so a reader new to the repository took “until it runs the checker” for a second meaning of the word, or a plan that the skill does not state. The bold rule now states only the fact, and the next sentence gives the plan, which is your decision P-12. The installed text wrote that sentence as “It is to run the checker”, which a worker could read as an order to itself. After the cold read it reads “Walk will run the checker”.

Change 25 · interpreter.md, “What walk checks”A new kind of pair checked by the overloading rules

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

interpreter.md, “What walk checks”, line 43, the third of the pairs that keep the team's check

  • a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one;, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;

Why. The batch made walk check a new kind of pair by the overloading rules on declared domains: a generic function beside a functional method of a generic trait or object, where the method has no static parameters of its own. Walk now reads such a pair as two generic declarations. The list of the pairs that keep the team's old check still held it, so a worker would expect the team's message, not the name of the broken rule. The pair now leaves that list. The first wording, “a functional method of a generic trait or object that has no static parameters of its own”, let the last clause attach to the trait, which then could not be generic. After the cold read it reads “a generic trait's or object's functional method that has”.

Change 26 · interpreter.md, “What walk checks”A fixed refusal gone, and the departure the fix opened

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

interpreter.md, “What walk checks”, line 53, among walk's departures from the rules

  • Where a program's own component declares both, it refuses a generic operator between an array of a number type and a number, on either side, beside the operator of a self-typed trait, as AdditiveGroup's +: “at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types”. The checker accepts such a pair, and the library's own pairs load (ledger row 804).
  • It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait T[\A\] and is not an A (revival-changes.md, “Traits and objects”). A call that both T's operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends T[\A\] an A.

Why. The first bullet said that walk refuses the self-typed pair in a program's own code. The batch fixed that, as change 20 says, so the bullet is gone. The fix opened a new departure, which the batch's skeptic found: walk now loads an object that extends a self-typed trait T[\A\] without being an A, which the specification makes a static error and the checker refuses. A call that two declarations fit, and neither more specifically, then runs one of them with no error. The new bullet says so. After the cold read, it adds that no ambiguity error comes, and what to do: make each such type an A, so that no worker relies on the declaration that walk happens to pick.

Change 27 · interpreter.md, “What walk checks”A function that walk loads and the checker refuses

New text; underlined, what was added

interpreter.md, “What walk checks”, line 54, a new departure

  • It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: ‘… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method’ (ledger row 894).

Why. The skeptic found a second case where the paths now differ. Since the fix, walk loads a generic top-level function, such as a + over a subtype, whose domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's operator of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses it, by a check that the specification does not state; the ledger marks the row as contested. The first wording, “a generic function inside the declared domain”, could be read as a function declared inside the method. It now says “a top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of” the method. The cold read asked how a worker would recognise the checker's refusal, so the bullet now names the checker's check and quotes its message. The first wording also said that no decision yet says which path is right. That is a decision's status, which goes stale, so it was cut.

Change 28 · interpreter.md, “Natives”Which declared string types walk carries for a helper

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

interpreter.md, “Natives”, line 96, the second bullet of the Java types of a helper's binding

  • String, FlatString and JavaString in String;, and String too, except as a parameter other than self; ZZ in BigInteger; () in void.

interpreter.md, “Natives”, line 100, the first bullet of the Java types of self

  • a type of the list above, except FlatString, JavaString and (), in the same Java type;, but FlatString only where it is the library's own;

interpreter.md, “Natives”, line 108, the second of walk's refusals at load

  • The result type, or a parameter type other than self's, is not in carried by the first list: ‘no Java type carries the declared’.

Why. The batch changed which types walk carries for a helper's binding. A parameter declared String, other than self, is now refused at load, because a string that || builds would reach the native as the name of its type, not its text. A result or self of type String is still carried. And self of the library's own FlatString is now carried, so eleven of its methods bind helpers. The lists said that String is always carried, and FlatString never as self. They now say both. The refusal said “not in the first list”, but String is in the list and is still refused as a parameter, so it now reads “not carried by the first list”.

Change 29 · interpreter.md, “Natives”A program's own type named FlatString

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

interpreter.md, “Natives”, line 103

A program can give its own type the name FlatString or JavaString, so these names carry no self. So a binding in a method of the library's FlatString cannot name a helper yet: every program would stop at load.. Walk tells the library's FlatString by the component that declares it, so a program's own type of either name carries no self. But walk carries a parameter declared at such a type in String, by the type's name alone, and does not refuse the binding. The native then receives the name of the type, not the value's text (ledger row 877). Give a program's own type another name.

Why. The old text said that a method of the library's FlatString cannot bind a helper, since every program would stop at load. That is no longer true: walk now tells the library's FlatString by the component that declares it, and eleven of its methods bind helpers. A program's own type of that name still carries no self. The skill writer added a trap that sits in the same place. A parameter declared at a program's own FlatString is still carried by the type's name, so the native gets the name of the type instead of the text, and nothing refuses it. After the cold read, the text says plainly that no refusal comes and that the text is wrong, and what to do: give the program's type another name.

Change 30 · interpreter.md, “Natives”The natives that still get a CatString wrong, and the library's form

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

interpreter.md, “Natives”, line 117

A native declared over String, glue class or helper alike, receives A glue class bound over String, and a helper bound in a method of String as self, receive the wrong text for a CatString, as a parameter or as self in a method of String: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). || builds a CatString when the joined string is longer than maxLeafSize, 32 characters by default. If a string that reaches such a native can come from ||, pass it as s.asFlatString at the call of the native. In a method of String, call a function that binds the helper, with self.asFlatString. Bind such a native over FlatString, and beside it an overload over String that passes s.asFlatString, as printlnWithThread does (Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4640-4644). In a method of String, call that overload with self.

Why. Since a helper's String parameter is now refused at load (change 28), a helper can no longer receive a CatString as a parameter. Two cases still get the wrong text: a glue class bound over String, and a helper bound as self in a method of String. The old text named every native over String alike. Its advice was to convert the string at each call of the native, which every caller must remember. The text now gives the library's own form: the native over FlatString, and an overload over String that converts once. The first rewrite dropped the advice for a method of String; after the cold read, the text says to call that overload with self.

Change 31 · compiler.md, “What the compiled path cannot compile yet”Local functions now compile, but for three forms

New text; underlined, the words that changed; struck through, the words that went

compiler.md, “What the compiled path cannot compile yet”, lines 40 to 48

  • label and exit, spawn, and atomic used as an expression;
  • a local function declaration, and an object expression;
  • an array literal, such as [1 2 3].

It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):

  • a local function with static parameters of its own: ‘Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet’;
  • two local functions of one name in a block: ‘Can't compile overloaded local functions yet’;
  • a local function with the atomic modifier: ‘Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet’.

Why. The batch taught the code generator to compile a local function: it builds a closure. The list still named local functions among the constructs that it has no case for, so a worker would have avoided them in compiled code, or recorded as a failure a form that now compiles. The text now says that a local function compiles, and lists the three forms that the code generator still refuses. After the cold read, each form carries its message, so that a worker can tell such a refusal from another failure and name it in a test that records it. The text also says that a local function that calls another of its block compiles, which the first wording left open.

Change 32 · compiler.md, “Natives”A helper class with a type that only the compiler's prelude has

New text; underlined, what was added

compiler.md, “Natives”, line 96, the paragraph on the wrapper generator

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. nativeHelpers/systemOps is such a class: its getArgs answers StringVector, so the message is ‘FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.’ (ledger row 895). Bind a helper of another class.

Why. The paragraph said that every method of a helper class must map to Fortress, but not that, in the two stages that check the interpreter's library, it is that library which decides what maps. The batch found the case: one method of systemOps answers StringVector, a type that only the compiler's prelude declares, so a binding of any helper of that class stops its whole component. The first wording named only that class, without the reason, so a worker could bind a helper of another class with the same flaw. After the cold read, the text gives the general rule, why systemOps falls under it, what the distance stage then counts, and what to do: bind a helper of another class.
